Description

The documentation for `cp.array` says

> blocking ([bool](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#bool)) – Default is False, meaning if a H2D copy is needed it would run asynchronously on the current stream, and users are responsible for ensuring the stream order. For example, writing to the source obj without proper ordering while copying would result in a race condition. If set to True, the copy is synchronous (with respect to the host).

However, this doesn't mention that the function doesn't keep the source obj alive while the asynchronous copy happens. So even if you don't modify the data through `obj`, simply releasing the last reference to `obj` can cause it to be garbage collected, and the memory can then be reallocated from the memory pool (or from a lower level, if not using a pool).

This is mostly a risk when `obj` is backed by pinned memory (which is where I got bitten by this, and spent a few days chasing the race condition). Looking at the source code, when the `obj` is pinned, a temporary transfer buffer is allocated (`_alloc_async_transfer_buffer`) and the data is synchronously copied to that buffer, in which case there is no risk. However, if allocation of the transfer buffer fails, the fallback path directly does an asynchronous copy from the source data, and the risk remains, so this is not purely something people allocating their own pinned memory need to be concerned about.

Right after `copy_from_host_async` here:
https://github.com/cupy/cupy/blob/118ade4a146d1cc68519f7f661f2c145f0b942c9/cupy/_core/core.pyx#L2588-L2589
we should add `pinned_memory._add_to_watch_list(stream.record(), a_cpu)` to ensure we hold a reference to `obj` as suggested @bmerry. 

A potential concern is that the watcher's `check_and_release` method is not called until next time we allocate pinned memory (through CuPy!), so the reference could be held longer than needed. We might want to consider documenting how to manually release it, similar to `free_all_blocks` for GPU memory.

In the long-term, I would suggest to use the same stream-ordered memory pool for pinned memory too, so that the lifetime management becomes moot. PR has the following changes: - Removes duplicate keys in the yaml (by moving logic to jinja) in order to appease the linter - Adds the sysctkXX extras name to the pip install command - Adds a patch to fix search paths for curand in conda environments - Adds import tests to most of the packages - Adds pip check to the tests - Runs a few tests from the examples for the CPU metapackage - Removes cupy-core from the base package requirements so that GPU-less users can use the GPU API without cupy - Adds meta-package dependencies to run_contrained of the main package - Converts the dx meta-package to noarch: generic Closes #8 - Adds a cpu meta-package which is not noarch because the dependencies differ based on the platform - Adds descriptions to the meta-packages - Moves aarch PR has the following changes: - Removes duplicate keys in the yaml (by moving logic to jinja) in order to appease the linter - Adds the sysctkXX extras name to the pip install command - Adds a patch cupy-core from the base package requirements so that GPU-less users can use the GPU API without cupy - Adds meta-package dependencies to run_contrained of the main package - Converts the dx meta-package to noarch: generic Closes #8 - Adds a cpu meta-package which is not noarch because the dependencies differ based on the platform - Adds descriptions to the meta-packages - Moves aarch been established by the array API standard and DLPack maintainers that users should just use the one-shot function call
```python
arr2 = array_namespace.from_dlpack(arr1)
```
as a (possibly zero-copy) array constructor through the DLPack protocol. Importantly, the capsule should be kept as implementation detail, not exposed to end users. This also allows safer handshaking (correct stream ordering and lifetime management).

The fact that various libraries still keep the legacy, capsule-exposing APIs to me is a maintenance burden, hard to teach, and already causing confusions (ex: https://github.com/dmlc/dlpack/issues/147 is coming from users who have no idea about the new things).

CuPy already marked the old, capsule-consuming API `cupy.fromDlpack()` deprecated, but unfortunately the old, capsule-exposing `cupy.ndarray.toDlpack()` was not yet marked as deprecated. We also have not taught about the new practice in the Interoperability page.

I suggest 
1. we deprecate and remove both in v14 or v15 (I prefer aggressively, but it does not have to be)

PR has the following changes: - Removes duplicate keys in the yaml (by moving logic to jinja) in order to appease the linter - Adds the sysctkXX extras name to the pip install command - Adds a patch to fix search paths for curand in conda environments - Adds import tests to most of the packages - Adds pip check to the tests - Runs a few tests from the examples for the CPU metapackage - Removes cupy-core from the base package requirements so that GPU-less users can use the GPU API without cupy - Adds meta-package dependencies to run_contrained of the main package - Converts the dx meta-package to noarch: generic Closes #8 - Adds a cpu meta-package which is not noarch because the dependencies differ based on the platform - Adds descriptions to the meta-packages - Moves aarch from cross-compile to full emulation in order to provide correct environment for runtime detection of CTK headers. Description

I am getting weird `CUDA_ERROR_COOPERATIVE_LAUNCH_TOO_LARGE: too many blocks in cooperative launch` and `CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_CLUSTER_SIZE: a kernel launch error has occurred due to cluster misconfiguration` errors when I try out kernels with `__cluster_dims__` annotations. The number of blocks I am launching should be entirely sufficient for the GPU. In particular I am getting `CUDA_ERROR_COOPERATIVE_LAUNCH_TOO_LARGE` when I try to use a cluster size of 16, and the other when I try 8 or less.

### To Reproduce

```py
kernel = r"""
extern "C" __global__ void __cluster_dims__(4,1,1) entry0() {
    return ;
}
"""
import cupy as cp

raw_module = cp.RawModule(code=kernel, backend='nvcc', enable_cooperative_groups=True)
def main():
    v9 = raw_module.get_function(f"entry0")
    v9.max_dynamic_shared_size_bytes = 229376 
    v9((128,),(256,),(),shared_mem=229376)
    return 

if __name__ == '__main__': print(main())
```

+DLPack data exchange protocol
+-----------------------------
 
 `DLPack <https://github.com/dmlc/dlpack>`__ is a specification of tensor structure to share tensors among frameworks.

### Issue

This is a followup to https://github.com/conda-forge/cuda-nvcc-feedstock/issues/56 and https://github.com/conda-forge/cuda-feedstock/issues/58.  Unlike the other two issues, all packages have been installed using the conda-forge channel.


We are trying to build FBGEMM against the CUDA 12.6 (https://github.com/pytorch/FBGEMM/pull/3503), and are running into the following error:

```
-- Could NOT find CUDA (missing: CUDA_INCLUDE_DIRS) (found version "12.6")
CMake Warning at /github/home/miniconda/envs/build_binary/lib/python3.13/site-packages/torch/share/cmake/Caffe2/public/cuda.cmake:31 (message):
  PyTorch: CUDA cannot be found.  Depending on whether you are building
  PyTorch or a PyTorch dependent library, the next warning / error will give
  you more info.
Call Stack (most recent call first):
  /github/home/miniconda/envs/build_binary/lib/python3.13/site-packages/torch/share/cmake/Caffe2/Caffe2Config.cmake:86 (include)
  /github/home/miniconda/envs/build_binary/lib/python3.13/site-packages/torch/share/cmake/Torch/TorchConfig.cmake:68 (find_package)
  /__w/FBGEMM/FBGEMM/cmake/modules/PyTorchSetup.cmake:14 (find_package)
  CMakeLists.txt:78 (include)
```

Contrary to https://github.com/conda-forge/cuda-nvcc-feedstock/issues/56, we are now installing CUDA using the conda-forge channel, i.e.

```
conda install --force-reinstall -n build_env -c conda-forge -y cuda=12.6.3
```

We did notice that for CUDA 12.6, when we look for `cuda.h`, we see:

```
(base) bash-5.2# find / -name cuda.h
/root/miniconda/envs/build_env/x86_64-conda-linux-gnu/sysroot/usr/include/linux/cuda.h
/root/miniconda/envs/build_env/targets/x86_64-linux/include/cuda.h
/root/miniconda/pkgs/cuda-cudart-dev_linux-64-12.4.127-h85509e4_2/targets/x86_64-linux/include/cuda.h
/root/miniconda/pkgs/kernel-headers_linux-64-3.10.0-he073ed8_18/x86_64-conda-linux-gnu/sysroot/usr/include/linux/cuda.h
```

likewise with CUDA 12.4, we have:

```
(base) bash-5.2# find / -name cuda.h
/root/miniconda/envs/build_env/x86_64-conda-linux-gnu/sysroot/usr/include/linux/cuda.h
/root/miniconda/envs/build_env/targets/x86_64-linux/include/cuda.h
/root/miniconda/pkgs/cuda-cudart-dev_linux-64-12.6.77-h3f2d84a_0/targets/x86_64-linux/include/cuda.h
/root/miniconda/pkgs/kernel-headers_linux-64-3.10.0-he073ed8_18/x86_64-conda-linux-gnu/sysroot/usr/include/linux/cuda.h
```

Note that if we install CUDA 12.4 using the nvidia channel for example, i.e.:

```
conda install --force-reinstall -n build_env -c "nvidia/label/cuda-12.4.1" -y cuda
```

then we get:

```
(base) bash-5.2# find / -name cuda.h
/root/miniconda/envs/build_env/x86_64-conda-linux-gnu/sysroot/usr/include/linux/cuda.h
/root/miniconda/envs/build_env/include/cuda.h
/root/miniconda/pkgs/cuda-cudart-dev-12.4.127-0/include/cuda.h
/root/miniconda/pkgs/kernel-headers_linux-64-3.10.0-he073ed8_18/x86_64-conda-linux-gnu/sysroot/usr/include/linux/cuda.h
```

In other words, when installing using conda-forge, the CUDA headers do not appear to be installed onto `$CONDA_PREFIX/include`, which seems to be the reason that cmake is unable to find the path.

How do we resolve this?

I made a judgement call in a few things:
1. Raise ~~`UserWarning`~~ **`VisibleDeprecationWarning`** in both functions to make it more noisy 
   - We've raised `DeprecationWarning` in `fromDlpack` for a long time. Since it does not make sense to only deprecate in one direction and not both, the assumption here is users should already expect the deprecation.
   - Also note that apparently we have a lot of docs teaching about `from_dlpack` already (which is great!)
2. Replace the (likely outdated) TensorFlow example in favor of a Jax one
   - This makes the example easier to follow and more unified (all major array libraries do the same thing now)

I made a judgement call in a few things:
1. Raise ~~`UserWarning`~~ **`VisibleDeprecationWarning`** in both functions to make it more noisy 
   - We've raised `DeprecationWarning` in `fromDlpack` for a long time. Since it does not make sense to only deprecate in one direction and not both, the assumption here is users should already expect the deprecation.
   - Also note that apparently we have a lot of docs teaching about `from_dlpack` already (which is great!)
2. Replace the (likely outdated) TensorFlow example in favor of a Jax one
   - This makes the example easier to follow and more unified (all major array libraries do the same thing now)

Description

I am getting weird `CUDA_ERROR_COOPERATIVE_LAUNCH_TOO_LARGE: too many blocks in cooperative launch` and `CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_CLUSTER_SIZE: a kernel launch error has occurred due to cluster misconfiguration` errors when I try out kernels with `__cluster_dims__` annotations. The number of blocks I am launching should be entirely sufficient for the GPU. In particular I am getting `CUDA_ERROR_COOPERATIVE_LAUNCH_TOO_LARGE` when I try to use a cluster size of 16, and the other when I try 8 or less.

### To Reproduce

```py
kernel = r"""
extern "C" __global__ void __cluster_dims__(4,1,1) entry0() {
    return ;
}
"""
import cupy as cp

raw_module = cp.RawModule(code=kernel, backend='nvcc', enable_cooperative_groups=True)
def main():
    v9 = raw_module.get_function(f"entry0")
    v9.max_dynamic_shared_size_bytes = 229376 
    v9((128,),(256,),(),shared_mem=229376)
    return 

if __name__ == '__main__': print(main())
```

## Guidelines for marking packages as broken:

* We prefer to patch the repo data (see [here](https://github.com/conda-forge/conda-forge-repodata-patches-feedstock))
  instead of marking packages as broken. This alternative workflow makes environments more reproducible.
* Packages with requirements/metadata that are too strict but otherwise work are
  not technically broken and should not be marked as such.
* Packages with missing metadata can be marked as broken on a temporary basis
  but should be patched in the repo data and be marked unbroken later.
* In some cases where the number of users of a package is small or it is used by
  the maintainers only, we can allow packages to be marked broken more liberally.
* We (`conda-forge/core`) try to make a decision on these requests within 24 hours.

What will happen when a package is marked broken?

* Our bots will add the `broken` label to the package. The `main` label will remain on the package and this is normal.
* Our bots will rebuild our repodata patches to remove this package from the repodata.
* In a few hours after the `anaconda.org` CDN picks up the new patches, you will no longer be able to install the package from the `main` channel.


## Checklist:

* [ ] I want to mark a package as broken (or not broken):
  * [ ] Added a description of the problem with the package in the PR description.

* [ ] I want to copy an artifact following [CFEP-3](https://github.com/conda-forge/cfep/blob/main/cfep-03.md):

  * [ ] Added a reference to the original PR

* [x] I want to add a package output to a feedstock:
  * [x] Pinged the relevant feedstock team(s)
  * [x] Added a small description of why the output is being added.

## Guidelines for marking packages as broken:

* We prefer to patch the repo data (see [here](https://github.com/conda-forge/conda-forge-repodata-patches-feedstock))
  instead of marking packages as broken. This alternative workflow makes environments more reproducible.
* Packages with requirements/metadata that are too strict but otherwise work are
  not technically broken and should not be marked as such.
* Packages with missing metadata can be marked as broken on a temporary basis
  but should be patched in the repo data and be marked unbroken later.
* In some cases where the number of users of a package is small or it is used by
  the maintainers only, we can allow packages to be marked broken more liberally.
* We (`conda-forge/core`) try to make a decision on these requests within 24 hours.

What will happen when a package is marked broken?

* Our bots will add the `broken` label to the package. The `main` label will remain on the package and this is normal.
* Our bots will rebuild our repodata patches to remove this package from the repodata.
* In a few hours after the `anaconda.org` CDN picks up the new patches, you will no longer be able to install the package from the `main` channel.


## Checklist:

* [ ] I want to mark a package as broken (or not broken):
  * [ ] Added a description of the problem with the package in the PR description.
  * [ ] Pinged the team for the package for their input.

* [ ] I want to archive a feedstock:
  * [ ] Pinged the team for that feedstock for their input.
  * [ ] Make sure you have opened an issue on the feedstock explaining why it was archived.
  * [ ] Linked that issue in this PR description.
  * [ ] Added links to any other relevant issues/PRs in the PR description.

* [ ] I want to request (or revoke) access to an opt-in CI resource:
  * [ ] Pinged the relevant feedstock team(s)
  * [ ] Added a small description explaining why access is needed

* [ ] I want to copy an artifact following [CFEP-3](https://github.com/conda-forge/cfep/blob/main/cfep-03.md):
  * [ ] Pinged the relevant feedstock team(s)
  * [ ] Added a reference to the original PR
  * [ ] Posted a link to the conda artifacts
  * [ ] Posted a link to the build logs

* [x] I want to add a package output to a feedstock:
  * [x] Pinged the relevant feedstock team(s)
  * [x] Added a small description of why the output is being added.

Your question:

## The problem

For packages built with pybind11 and nanobind, the major version of the C++ compiler is part of the ABI. That means any package built with nanobind that _links_ to another package via its nanobind API has a runtime requirement that both were built with the same major version of the compiler. This is not currently handled by the `pybind11-abi` metapackage or other compiler run_exports.

I don't think it comes up very often, but it does in the fenics stack. For fenics, I've added a `fenics-basix-nanobind-abi` package with a custom version that includes the nanobind and cxx_compiler versions. In the past, I had the same that bundled the pybind11-abi version and compiler version. I've only made one of these because everything in fenics depends on basix, but technically every package build with nanobind (that might be linked against in `host`) should have one.  But this is a general problem, if not a common one. pybind11 has a `pybind11-abi` package, and nanobind [will soon as well](https://github.com/conda-forge/nanobind-feedstock/pull/15). But this is only half a solution, because it doesn't take the build-time compiler version into account, which is also part of the ABI in packages built with either pybind11 or nanobind.

My `fenics-basix-nanobind-abi` approach also doesn't solve the problem as well as I'd like because downstream packages _build_ just fine since the compiler version is not actually restricted in the build env, but they won't import. that means e.g. cross-compiled outputs pass all CI when they are completely broken, when really the build should have been prevented in the first place due to the compiler version conflict.

Also, I've only dealt with this on linux/mac and don't actually know what needs to be restricted on Windows.


## Question

I've struggled to come up with a general solution, but it seems like having `nanobind` or `pybind11` in host dependencies should:

1. restrict the C++ compiler version at build time when in host requirements, and
2. restrict install-time packages to those built with the same C++ compiler
 
One hard part is that pybind11/nanobind packages are host dependencies, so can't easily restrict the cxx compiler version in the build environment. Is there a package in the host env that could be used as a proxy? Or should we be adding a metapackage to the build env to keep things in sync?

Does anyone have a recommendation/experience for a best practice for ensuring ABI compatibility that is sensitive to the compiler version? Is defining one of these abi metapackage outputs for every nanobind-built package really the way to go?

## Possible solution

My only idea so far for a general solution is to update the `pybind11/nanobind-abi` packages (or separately add `nanobind-cxx-abi`) to generate a version for each compiler version with run_constrains on the compiler version and nanobind and strong run_exports on itself.

so e.g. `nanobind-cxx-abi 0.13.12 gxx_*` would have:

where:
 
- 0 is the versioning scheme (increment when we change how it works)
- 13 is the nanobind internals version
- 12 is `cxx_compiler_version`
- `gxx` is `cxx_compiler`

and would look something like:

```yaml
run_exports:
  strong:
    - {{ pin_subpackage('nanobind-cxx-abi', max_pin='x.x.x.x') }} {{ cxx_compiler }}_*
run_constrained:
  # constrain compiler version (only works if it's in the build env)
  - {{ cxx_compiler }}_impl_{{ target_platform }} {{ cxx_compiler_version }}.*
  # constrain nanobind abi (host env)
  - nanobind-abi {{ nanobind_internals_version }}
  # another compiler constraint that would work on the host env? libstdcxx_devel?
```

and then packages make sure this is the same version in both the build and host requirements. * https://pypi.org/project/cuda-python/12.6.1/

## Guidelines for marking packages as broken:

* We prefer to patch the repo data (see [here](https://github.com/conda-forge/conda-forge-repodata-patches-feedstock))

  but should be patched in the repo data and be marked unbroken later.

  the maintainers only, we can allow packages to be marked broken more liberally.
* We (`conda-forge/core`) try to make a decision on these requests within 24 hours.

* Our bots will add the `broken` label to the package. The `main` label will remain on the package and this is normal.
* Our bots will rebuild our repodata patches to remove this package from the repodata.
* In a few hours after the `anaconda.org` CDN picks up the new patches, you will no longer be able to install the package from the `main` channel.

Description

Using either NVCC or NVRTC backends, my kernels cannot include system wide headers on windows 11 with CUDA 12.4 / MSVC 143 (x64).
Altough it build fine on a normal Visual Studio CUDA project.


### To Reproduce

Example to demonstrate that system-wide headers are not included

```py
import cupy as cp

CUDA_MAX_THREADS_PER_BLOCK = 512

kernel = cp.RawKernel(r"""
#include <cfloat>

#define F_MAX FLT_MAX

extern "C" __global__ void test(int n, double *a, double *b, float *c)
{
    int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    if (i < n)
    {
        double r = a[i] + b[i];
        if (r > F_MAX)
            r = F_MAX;
        c[i] = r;
    }
}
""","test")

n = 1024
res = cp.zeros((n,), dtype=cp.float32)
a = cp.full((n,), 1.0, dtype=cp.float64)
b = cp.full((n,), 2.0, dtype=cp.float64)
kernel(
    ((n + CUDA_MAX_THREADS_PER_BLOCK - 1) // CUDA_MAX_THREADS_PER_BLOCK,),
    (CUDA_MAX_THREADS_PER_BLOCK,),
    (n, a, b, res),
)

assert cp.all(res == 3.0)
```

Error output:
error: identifier "FLT_MAX" is undefined

## Guidelines for marking packages as broken:

* We prefer to patch the repo data (see [here](https://github.com/conda-forge/conda-forge-repodata-patches-feedstock))
  instead of marking packages as broken. This alternative workflow makes environments more reproducible.
* Packages with requirements/metadata that are too strict but otherwise work are
  not technically broken and should not be marked as such.
* Packages with missing metadata can be marked as broken on a temporary basis
  but should be patched in the repo data and be marked unbroken later.
* In some cases where the number of users of a package is small or it is used by
  the maintainers only, we can allow packages to be marked broken more liberally.
* We (`conda-forge/core`) try to make a decision on these requests within 24 hours.

What will happen when a package is marked broken?

* Our bots will add the `broken` label to the package. The `main` label will remain on the package and this is normal.
* Our bots will rebuild our repodata patches to remove this package from the repodata.
* In a few hours after the `anaconda.org` CDN picks up the new patches, you will no longer be able to install the package from the `main` channel.

12.6.1 release of cuda-python introduced a new package layout in the form of the cuda/bindings directory. For backwards compatibility, the old modules were preserved in their original locations but raise warnings indicating that the old layout is deprecated. Due to https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuda-python/issues/215 we had to yank that release and get a new one up to fix it. 12.6.2 seems to have resolved this issue, but there is still something off. This time the issue appears to be specific to the conda-forge package (neither the nvidia channel's conda package nor the wheel on PyPI exhibit this issue).

This script demonstrates the issue:
```
mamba create -y -n test_cuda_python python=3.11 -c conda-forge > /dev/null                                                                                                            
conda activate test_cuda_python                                                                                                                                                       
pip install  cuda-python==12.6.2 > /dev/null                                                                                                                                          
echo -n "Checking if ccudart is in the wheel: "                                                                                                                                       
ls $(python -c 'import site; print(site.getsitepackages()[0])')/cuda/ | grep ccudart.pxd || echo ""                                                                                   
pip uninstall -y cuda-python > /dev/null                                                                                                                                              
mamba install -y cuda-python==12.6.2 -c conda-forge > /dev/null                                                                                                                       
echo -n "Checking if ccudart is in the conda-forge conda package: "                                                                                                                   
ls $(python -c 'import site; print(site.getsitepackages()[0])')/cuda/ | grep ccudart.pxd || echo ""                                                                                   
mamba uninstall -y cuda-python > /dev/null                                                                                                                                            
mamba install -y cuda-python==12.6.2 -c nvidia -c conda-forge > /dev/null                                                                                                             
echo -n "Checking if ccudart is in the nvidia conda package: "                                                                                                                        
ls $(python -c 'import site; print(site.getsitepackages()[0])')/cuda/ | grep ccudart.pxd || echo ""                                                                                   
conda deactivate                                                                                                                                                                      
conda env remove -n test_cuda_python > /dev/null  
```

This script outputs
```
Checking if ccudart is in the wheel: ccudart.pxd
Checking if ccudart is in the conda-forge conda package: 
Checking if ccudart is in the nvidia conda package: ccudart.pxd
```

The same is true for all the pxd files that should be in the top-level cuda directory. 

The build script for this feedstock does [a simple pip install](https://github.com/conda-forge/cuda-python-feedstock/blob/main/recipe/meta.yaml#L31). When I do the same locally, I also wind up without the extra top-level files. Description

`cupy.array_api.linalg.vecdot` does not behave the same as `np.linalg.vecdot` or `jax.numpy.linalg.vecdot` (or even `cupy.dot`) even when identical arguments are passed to these functions. The `cupy.array_api` function throws a shape error (`ValueError`) in the example below, whereas the other implementations don't.

I am aware that there are subtle differences between NumPy and CuPy, so I am not sure if this is a bug or if this is intended. It looks like a bug as passing the same arguments to `cupy.dot` works, but `cupy.array_api.linalg.vecdot(..., axis=1)` (should behave as `dot`) doesn't.

### To Reproduce

## Array API compatible NumPy implementation (works)
```py
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=42)

a = rng.standard_normal((100, 20))
b = rng.standard_normal((100,))

_, n = a.shape
x = np.zeros(n)

w = np.linalg.vecdot(b - a @ x, a, axis=0)  # works
```

## Array API compatible JAX implementation (works)
```py
import numpy as np
import jax.numpy as jnp

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=42)

a = rng.standard_normal((100, 20))
b = rng.standard_normal((100,))

a_j = jnp.array(a)
b_j = jnp.array(b)

_, n_j = a_j.shape
x_j = jnp.zeros(n_j)

w_j = jnp.linalg.vecdot(b_j - a_j @ x_j, a_j, axis=0)  # works
```

## Array API non-compatible CuPy (works)

Using `dot` instead of `linalg.vecdot(..., axis=1)` as the latter does not exist -

```py
import numpy as np
import cupy

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=42)

a = rng.standard_normal((100, 20))
b = rng.standard_normal((100,))

a_cu = cupy.asarray(a)
b_cu = cupy.asarray(b)

_, n_cu = a_cu.shape
x_cu = cupy.zeros(n_cu)

w_cu = cupy.dot(b_cu - a_cu @ x_cu, a_cu)  # works
```

## Array API compatible CuPy (does not work)
```py
import numpy as np
import cupy.array_api as cp

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=42)

a = rng.standard_normal((100, 20))
b = rng.standard_normal((100,))

a_c = cp.asarray(a)
b_c = cp.asarray(b)

_, n_c = a_c.shape
x_c = cp.zeros(n_c)

w_c = cp.linalg.vecdot(b_c - a_c @ x_c, a_c, axis=0)  # does not work

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/121975

upon interpreter exit and using `RandomState`, the following exception can occur

```python
Exception ignored in: <function RandomState.__del__ at 0x7f0cc41dadd0>
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/coder/.conda/envs/rapids/lib/python3.10/site-packages/cupy/random/_generator.py", line 65, in __del__
ModuleNotFoundError: import of cupy_backends.cuda.libs halted; None in sys.modules

Description

Iteratively constructing an array via `xp.concatenate` appears to leak memory on a Jetson Orin Nano, running JetPack 5.1.3. (See the loop below). While the resident set size reported by `ps` remains below 1 MB, the GPU memory use reported in `/sys/kernel/debug/nvmap/iovmm/clients` climbs past 300 MB, eventually crashing the device if run for enough iterations.

### To Reproduce

The following loop causes GPU memory use by the Python process to exceed 300 MB:

```py
import time
import cupy as xp

array = xp.empty(0, dtype=xp.float64)
for i in range(1000):
    new_data = xp.random.rand(60)
    array = xp.concatenate([array, new_data])
    time.sleep(0.02)
```

In contrast, with pre-allocating the array, memory use is constant around 70 MB:

```py
import time
import cupy as xp

array = xp.empty(60000, dtype=xp.float64)
for i in range(1000):
    new_data = xp.random.rand(60)
    array[60*i:60*(i+1)] = new_data
    time.sleep(0.02)
```

### Installation

Wheel (`pip install cupy-***`)

The lines [here](https://github.com/cupy/cupy/blob/9ec472c66555eaa277edb83ff3f907a73c950fde/cupy/cuda/compiler.py#L102)  
```
        import setuptools
        vctools = setuptools.msvc.EnvironmentInfo(platform.machine()).VCTools
```

fail even if visual studio is installed when using setuptool>=74.0 because the init in `setuptools` does not seems to expose `msvc` anymore
we need to replace by 
```
        import setuptools.msvc
        vctools = setuptools.msvc.EnvironmentInfo(platform.machine()).VCTools
```

```
>>> from cupy import _environment
>>> _environment._get_include_dir_from_conda_or_wheel(12, 5)
['/home/dagardner/work/conda/envs/morpheus/targets/-linux/include', '/home/dagardner/work/conda/envs/morpheus/include']
```

One possible work-around would be to call `platform.machine()` on systems that return an empty string:
```
>>> import platform
>>> platform.processor()
''
>>> platform.machine()
'x86_64'
```

```
import cupy as cp
cp.array(cp.zeros((1,)))

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).

* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This means that `np.from_dlpack(cupy_arr, device="cpu")` works (with NumPy 2). Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This means that `np.from_dlpack(cupy_arr, device="cpu")` works (with NumPy 2).  The tests indirectly cover implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This means that `np.from_dlpack(cupy_arr, device="cpu")` works (with NumPy 2). implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This means that `np.from_dlpack(cupy_arr, device="cpu")` works (with NumPy 2). Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This is very tricky as I keep revisiting this part, and I'd like to share my understanding here to aid code review.

When this `toDlpack()` function was called, the producer/consumer streams are ordered, that's why we did not need to pass any stream argument. 

This is no longer true when CPU copy is requested. In the case of NumPy, [`stream=None` is provided](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/816fd7c0d1569bef00b3765d47528b093cf55839/numpy/_core/src/multiarray/dlpack.c#L536), but CuPy turns it to `streamLegacy` in `__dlpack__` and orders it after CuPy's current stream (whatever it is), so we're now on the consumer's (legacy) stream. implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This means that `np.from_dlpack(cupy_arr, device="cpu")` works (with NumPy 2).  The tests indirectly cover implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This means that `np.from_dlpack(cupy_arr, device="cpu")` works (with NumPy 2). * I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.
